entries.title: Calif kernel exploit: the author says it supports MIE.
entries.dek: Anna Groza says her upcoming kernel exploit works with Memory Integrity Enforcement (MIE), Apple’s newest memory protections. The code, the exact supported devices and iOS builds, and any independent check are still pending.
entries.scope: opa334 has discussed Dopamine support on A12/A13. The author says MIE is supported but has not listed the exact devices or builds.
observed: On November 3, Anna Groza (@pwnlambda) said she aims to release the iOS kernel read/write exploit and a write-up in about a week.
opa334 said separately that he expects to bring Dopamine, his jailbreak, to the exploit’s supported versions on A12/A13 devices using momentarius. He said A14 and newer still need a way past SPTM.
On November 4, she said the planned release is a working exploit with MIE support. She repeated the wait of about a week. She did not publish the code or a list of supported devices and builds.
entries.meaning: The researcher now says outright that the planned exploit works with MIE. When the code comes out, the first question is which protected devices it really covers. A kernel exploit alone is not a full jailbreak, and the claim does not include a way past SPTM (Secure Page Table Monitor), which guards memory above the kernel. opa334’s earlier comments about A12/A13 support are separate from what this exploit will actually support.
limits: This is a release plan. It is not a published exploit or a jailbreak release date.
MIE support is the author’s claim. We have not seen code, an explanation of how it works, a list of MIE devices and builds, or an independent reproduction.
Nothing shows that the coming exploit is the public AppleAVE2 temporal-layer PoC. Shared research credit does not mean they use the same bug or technique.

entries.title: A Calif demo survives an iOS update in Lockdown Mode.
entries.dek: Calif’s new video shows a tweak still working after an iOS update and restart, with iOS 27.2 on screen. Surviving an update is a different claim from breaking into a phone that already runs 27.2.
entries.scope: iPhone 18 Pro, according to MacRumors. The update ends with iOS 27.2 on screen.
observed: On November 3, Calif posted a three-minute video captioned “Lockdown Mode helps, until it doesn’t.” It shows a tweak working, the phone updating and restarting, and the tweak working again.
MacRumors reports that the phone is an iPhone 18 Pro and that the attack starts with a PDF accepted over AirDrop.

On November 4, Calif researcher Stefan Esser said not to assume the team’s videos all use one exploit chain. He said bug details will stay private until a fix ships, a fix is refused, or a fix takes unreasonably long.

In a public post the same day, Esser said they chose AirDrop so the PDF would open in Preview. He said Preview runs with Memory Tagging Extension (MTE), a hardware check that catches many memory bugs, when Lockdown Mode is on. This is his explanation of the demo setup, not something we measured.
entries.meaning: Surviving an update matters because the bug used to get in may already be fixed. The video supports a persistence demo on the device shown. It does not show how the tweak comes back after the update.
limits: The video does not show a fresh attack on a stock phone that already runs iOS 27.2.
We have not seen public code, how the tweak survives the update, or a full list of supported devices.
We watched the public video. Nobody has reproduced it independently.
Esser’s post does not name the bugs or say which steps appear in which video. It does not say which private steps will be in the separately announced kernel exploit release.
The claim that Preview runs with MTE comes from Esser. We did not check Preview’s settings or reproduce the exploit. The post also does not say that every iOS process uses the same setting.

entries.title: Liter8 becomes a more useful iPhone 11 research setup.
entries.dek: Version 0.2.3 keeps Wi-Fi passwords across restarts and adds SFTP file transfer. The previous release added optional kernel memory access. It still needs a computer attached at every boot and is only tested on the base iPhone 11.
entries.scope: Base iPhone 11 (n104ap). Documented up to iOS 27.2 (24B119).
observed: v0.2.3 adds SFTP and SCP file transfer in normal boot. Wi-Fi passwords now survive restarts, even though the setup runs without the Secure Enclave (SEP), the security chip that handles keys and passcodes.

v0.2.2 added an optional tfp0 boot patch, which gives direct access to kernel memory. The author’s test notes show kernel reads and writes to a scratch area of memory on iOS 27.2 (24B119), including after a second boot.
The README lists only the base iPhone 11 as tested. The 11 Pro and Pro Max are still experimental, even though the release notes word it more broadly.
entries.meaning: The published code and test notes make this a useful, specialized research setup. Kernel access comes from patching the boot process with usbliter8. It is not a new exploit that gets from an app to the kernel on a normal, running phone.
limits: Every boot needs a Mac and DFU mode, a low-level recovery mode. Setup erases and restores the phone.
The Secure Enclave, passcode and cellular data still do not work, as documented. Calls and texts go through Wi-Fi Calling in this setup.
The published write test only touches scratch memory. It does not show writes to memory protected by SPTM.
We read the source and the author’s test notes. We have not run this setup ourselves.

entries.title: A Canon RAW decoder writes backward past its pixel buffer.
entries.dek: Project Zero shows how a bad size check makes the decoder write image data below its buffer. The report includes a crafted image and debugger output. The iOS 27 line is already fixed.
observed: A malformed Canon sRAW image passes a size check that uses signed math. A separate, unchecked count then makes the decoder step backward through rows instead of forward.
The decoder then writes color data from the file backward, below the start of the pixel buffer. The report matches debugger output and the crash address to that write.
The report includes a crafted CR2 file and names the original, unmodified file as a working control.
entries.meaning: The write runs in a straight line below the buffer. The image file influences the bytes written, and the location depends on where the buffer sits in memory. The report says this could risk code execution, but its published result is memory corruption, not a full attack chain.
limits: Project Zero reports this fixed in macOS and iOS 27. Apple also lists a fix for the older line in iOS 26.7.2.
This is not a way into iOS 27.0.1 or 27.2.
The public test ran on a Mac. We have not seen an equivalent way to deliver it on iPhone, or an exploit chain.

entries.title: A RAW image correction loop runs past its buffer.
entries.dek: A Phase One decoder trusts a length taken from the file. The new Project Zero report is easy to study because it includes a control file that differs by one tag, plus the measured crash.
observed: One part of a flat-field correction loop, a step that evens out brightness across the sensor, is missing the row-width limit that the next part enforces.
The file influences both how far the loop runs and the correction value for each row. The result is a limited 16-bit read-and-update that can run past the end of the decoded image buffer.
The report includes a crashing IIQ image and a control file that differs by a single tag, with loop measurements and a crash at the edge of the buffer.
entries.meaning: The control file shows exactly which missing check causes the bug, which is more useful than a crash alone. This is credible public memory-corruption research. The published test does not show freely chosen bytes, a chosen target address or code execution.
limits: Apple lists the bug as fixed in iOS 26.7 and the iOS 27 line.
New technical detail does not make this a new, unpatched way into iOS 27.
The test results for the exact build come from macOS. We did not reproduce it on an iPhone.

entries.title: A link preview draws a later image frame into a buffer sized for the first.
entries.dek: A detailed report traces a link received in Messages to writes outside an image buffer. It shows nearby memory being overwritten, not just a crash, but there is little control over where the writes land.
entries.scope: Detailed test: macOS 26.7 (25G229). The author also reports iPhone tests.
observed: LinkPresentation sizes a pixel buffer from the first frame of an image, then draws using the size of a later frame.

The report shows writes outside the buffer: a clear, image data, and changes to a neighboring IOSurface (a shared graphics buffer) that was in use. It also includes control files and a comparison with the patched build.
When tested with a received link, the bug triggers after the recipient loads the preview in Messages. The source was published October 29 and the detailed report October 30.
entries.meaning: This is a strong public report. It connects delivery from outside the device, a specific sizing mistake and measured memory damage. The file influences how far the write goes and what it writes. Memory layout decides which neighboring buffer gets hit.
limits: No write to a chosen address and no code execution chain is published.
The Messages trigger needs the preview to load. It should not be called a proven zero-click attack, meaning one that needs no action from the victim.
The most detailed evidence about the build and process comes from macOS. Do not assume the same privileges or protections on iPhone without matching evidence.
Apple lists fixes in iOS 26.7.2 and 27.2.

entries.title: A public AVE reproduction crashes the kernel.
entries.dek: Specific video-encoding calls and a crash log from a real device support a kernel crash. Useful kernel access and any way past Apple’s protections are still unproven.
observed: The app sets an oversized temporal-layer count through VideoToolbox, Apple’s video framework, and submits a frame to encode. The crash log names videocodecd and AppleAVE2, the video encoder driver.

The author describes the damage as a fixed value written at a fixed offset, with no arbitrary kernel read or write. The README includes an input that does not crash as a control, and says iOS 27.2 rejects the call.
The author credits the original discovery to Calif/Chollima and presents this project as a reproduction.
entries.meaning: A crash in the kernel’s video encoder driver makes this relevant to kernel research. A limited write can be useful, but the public code does not show a repeatable, useful change to memory that the system survives.
limits: The crash location, AppleAVE2 +0xDA78, shows where it crashed. It does not show control over where the write goes or which object was overwritten.
It does not show a way to read memory, real kernel access, a way past MIE or a full jailbreak.
We inspected the source and crash log. We did not confirm the exact CVE by comparing driver binaries, and we did not reproduce the crash on a device.

entries.title: A media service hands apps files they cannot open themselves.
entries.dek: The published app reads a file through a handle opened by a system service, even though opening the same path directly is denied. The access shown is mostly the media library.
observed: The PoC asks mediaplaybackd, a media system service, to open a path the app chooses. The reply contains an open file handle.
The source and logs show reads through that handle, including SQLite database content. Opening the same path directly is denied.
The files reachable in testing are mostly in the media library. Tested protected paths and tested writes are still denied.
entries.meaning: The author’s evidence shows a real but limited access-control bug. The service opens files with permissions the app does not have. Getting a file handle does not give the app control of the service or loosen its own sandbox.
limits: It does not show general file system access, running code in the service, or kernel access.
The list of tested paths is limited. It is not a full map of which files can and cannot be read.
The author reports that someone else found the same bug independently. Apple’s credit in its advisory does not independently confirm this reproduction.
Reported fixed in iOS 26.7.2 and 27.2.

entries.title: A CoreMedia PoC corrupts memory in the iPhone display service.
entries.dek: The November 2 source release overwrites a saved return address with chosen data and shows a limited one-byte write in backboardd, the iPhone display service. Pointer authentication stops the return-address attack.
entries.scope: Author’s evidence: iPhone19,4 (iPhone Duo), iOS 27.1 (24A94425). The exact QuartzCore build is identified.
observed: The published app and payload generator send malformed Dolby Vision video metadata through CoreAnimation into backboardd, the iPhone display service. The code and supporting files are all public.

The saved crash shows backboardd, started by launchd, on build 24A94425. Its saved return address holds the chosen repeated-byte value. Pointer authentication, which checks return addresses before they are used, stops execution at the return instruction.

A separate test receipt reports that the service kept running after a request to write a fixed byte. A later crash from the same process shows the value 1 where it was read back. The zero-value control ran in a different process, so this is not a before-and-after measurement of one process.
The release credits Ping-2o/duper-cves for finding the fix location and quietvoid/dovi_tool for building the payload. Apple credits 정우 하 (@0xfa11babe) and Chris Bailey / Short Circuit for the CVE.
entries.meaning: This is stronger than an unexplained crash. Data the attacker chooses reaches a saved return address, and a separate test supports a tightly limited write of the value 1. It is still a result inside one process’s memory. It does not complete a sandbox escape or a jailbreak.
limits: We read the source and the author’s evidence. The PoC was not run or independently reproduced.

The written value is always 1, and the target stays inside an existing 4 GB address range. The result that the service kept running comes from a redacted test receipt, and the zero control came from a different process.
It does not show general memory read or write, code execution, a way past pointer authentication, kernel access or a full jailbreak.

The repository calls its link to CVE-2026-112688 a likely match at the function level. Apple lists the CoreMedia fix in iOS 27.2 but has not confirmed this exact parser. The wider impact in Apple’s advisory is not something this PoC demonstrates.
